is poured out too familiarly. From the habit of familiarity they will begin to despise you, and to regard you as almost one of their own. For no reverence is paid to superiors if their life is confined among their subjects. The one who presides must surpass all others in a certain reverence of maturity, and wisely avoid excessive familiarity with his subjects. Indeed, the eminence of authority is broken down when it is indiscreetly mixed with the actions of subjects. Speak ill of no one, and take no scandal against anyone. It is shameful for a priest to defile his tongue with detraction, the tongue which, placed at the altar, is appointed to pray for all. Nor should you lend an ear to detractors, because the detractor and the willing listener are worthy of equal condemnation. For the one carries the devil on his tongue, the other in his ear. Let such a man learn not readily to detract, when he sees that you are unwilling to listen. Do not be hasty in speech, and do not stand in the company of detractors, because they are hateful to almighty God. Hedge your ears with thorns, lest you hear the words of detractors. Let no lie proceed from your mouth; let no foul speech come from you, but be a guardian of your tongue, lest you offend in speech. Do not be slothful and lazy, nor given over to sleep and idleness, but continually go forward in the fervor of the Holy Spirit, knowing that this is proper to a priest: to have care for the needy. Have gold not so that you may keep it, but so that you may distribute it in alms for the poor. Let the bellies of the hungry poor praise you, not the feasts of the belching rich. Let your table be with the poor and needy, for in such persons Christ is received, and the heavenly court is honored. Avoid the banquets of the proud rich, especially of the powerful, in which nothing is done concerning the salvation of souls, and nothing at all is discussed concerning spiritual conversation. Let your clothing be honorable, not costly. In giving alms, do not seek glory from men, but expect praise and reward from God alone. Be a father of the poor and a guardian of orphans.

Let no poor man depart from you unconsoled. Do not be a striker or quarrelsome among the people; injure no one wrongfully, but do good to all as much as you can, even to enemies. Never coddle sinners, but rebuke them as one who has received authority from God. Do not be a striker of the consciences of the people committed to you, nor utter the word of God indiscreetly, but with the moderation of piety. Be merciful to penitents, and do not break the bruised reed, knowing that you have undertaken the care of the weak, not of the strong. For it is better to send a penitent with compassion to purgatory than, by the austerity of the confessor, to consign one driven to despair to hell. Do not neglect to pray your canonical hours with reverence and devotion at the times appointed by the Church. Likewise, do not omit to recite the hours of blessed Mary ever virgin, the vigils of the dead, together with the other things owed by priestly order. Have care of your household in the fear of God; if you have a household, persuade it by word and example to preserve modesty and honor. Indeed, it harms a priest’s reputation among the people when the people speak ill of his household.

Let your speech be strengthened by the testimony of the Scriptures, because whatever is commanded apart from the holy Scriptures is despised with the same ease with which it is proved. I do not want you to imitate those who, without learning, often cite fables and phantoms of dreams in church, and are ignorant of the mysteries of the divine Scriptures. Brawling and garrulous priests, speaking without reason, do not edify the people; by empty speeches and Aesopian fables they labor to draw them into admiration of themselves. For it is a foolish and damnable abuse, with the Scriptures and the Gospel set aside, to teach the Christian people the fables of Aesop and the fabricated deeds of the Romans. Nor should you wonder if the unlearned people hear these things more gladly than the Scriptures, since you read that the apostle foretold this. “There will be a time,” he says, “when they will not endure sound doctrine, but according to their own desires they will heap up teachers for themselves, itching in their ears; and from the truth indeed they will turn their hearing away, but to fables they will be turned.” Hence Jerome says: “To roll out words and, by rapidity of speech, to create admiration for oneself among the unlearned crowd is the mark of unlearned men.” A worn brow of the interpre

[unclear] often what he does not know; and when he has persuaded others, he also arrogates to himself knowledge that he does not have. Nothing is so easy as to deceive the low and unlearned common crowd by fluency of tongue; it admires all the more whatever it does not understand. But you, speak the things that befit sound doctrine, and do not seek the applause of the inexperienced if you wish to find a place among the learned. Do not imprudently desire the care of souls, unless first you have learned justly to govern both yourself and others according to ecclesiastical ordinance. For the office of teaching the people is exposed to many dangers and is troubled by daily anxieties. For a ruler of souls must be without fault, as God’s steward: not proud, not wrathful, not given to wine, not a striker, not greedy for shameful gain, but hospitable, kindly, sober, just, holy, continent, embracing that faithful word which is according to doctrine, so that he may be able to exhort in sound doctrine and to refute those who contradict it. He who has been appointed ruler of souls must teach no less by example than by word. A thief, indeed, can accuse avarice; but no one can correct it except the man who does what he teaches. He is a dainty teacher who disputes about fasting with a full belly. Therefore life must be required before doctrine, because one teaches more fully by deed than by speech. For the most excellent kind of teaching is the demonstration of example. And indeed the Lord Jesus first acted, afterward taught. For in teaching he uses the greatest authority whose speech is confirmed by the witness of his work. The speech of a ruler is readily received by subjects if it is supported by honorable conduct. But he who teaches well and lives badly condemns himself by the sentence of his own mouth and does not turn his subjects away from bad instruction. Consider at the same time how dangerous the care of souls is, especially in these times, when iniquity abounds everywhere and the charity of many has grown cold. For the days are evil, and men are slow to justice; the whole world is set in wickedness, and faith on earth is rare. Amid these things the word of God is despised by the people, the instruction of the Christian religion is neglected, priestly authority is scorned. The life of the laity, liable to a thousand sins and crimes, neglects the remedies of penance, applies itself to deceits and frauds, and despises the admonitions of priests.

And unless the ruler of souls diligently announces to the people entrusted to him their crimes and the penalties owed to sinners, before God he will also be guilty of their blood. And after these things God will bring all things into judgment, where the shepherd of souls is compelled to render an account for each person; and if he has been negligent in this world, he is condemned more severely. Therefore it is safer humbly to flee the care and rule of souls than arrogantly to usurp it. For if each person in that dreadful judgment is scarcely sufficient to render an account of his own life, how will he answer for so many thousands entrusted to him? O how well he lives who lives for himself. It seems honorable and pleasant among men to live in this world as a bishop, abbot, pastor, or any prelate at all; but who will be able to think how terrible the end of the negligent man is? For a very harsh judgment will be made against those who preside, and the powerful will suffer torments powerfully. Behold, he who lives simply passes through, to whom no earthly honor is entrusted, to whom no care of souls is committed. For pastoral care is never without danger so long as one lives in this world. And the greatest of all dangers is when, the soul having been separated from the body by death, the earthly shepherd must be presented to God, the supreme shepherd, to give an account. Here now the moment of final damnation threatens, when an account of badly administered stewardship is demanded and the blood of many sheep is required from the hand of an unworthy shepherd. What then will an inexperienced shepherd be able to answer to the charges, he who was negligent in the care of the sheep? He must fall silent, because he has nothing to answer. Therefore, brother, if you consider yourself fit for the care of souls, if you are preparing to govern the church of Mernicensem, know that you are to be brought into judgment for these things, and according to the merit of your life will receive either glory or torment. But believe me, he dies secure who, leaving aside concern for others, lives for himself alone in the fear of God. For to whom much is entrusted, much also will be required from him. A priest, especially one having the care of souls, is God’s herald, to announce to the people the will of the Almighty and to heal sinners in the law of the Lord by words of rebuke. Therefore he must be learned and most steadfast, lest he either slip through ignorance or through inconstancy fear the hatred of the perverse. It is shameful

For it is, through fear of the people, to keep silent the words of God. A priest must make use of wine sparingly, lest, if he gives himself over to drinking bouts, he become a reproach among the people. For the Apostle condemns wine-bibbing priests, and the old law forbids them access to the altar. In the Council of Agde also it is read thus: Before all things drunkenness is to be avoided by clerics, for it is the tinder and nurse of all vices. And so he who is found to have been drunk, as his rank allows, is either to be removed from communion for the space of thirty days, or subjected to bodily punishment. For wine is a luxurious thing, and drunkenness brings reproach; everyone who is mingled with these will not be wise. He who burns without wine, with the heat of youth, and is inflamed by the warmth of the blood, and is of vigorous body, should flee wine as poison, lest, suffocated by a manifold conflagration, he fall into the filth of lust.

A stomach heated with wine stirs up desire, dulls the senses, and weakens the head and the whole body. A fat belly begets a thin understanding. Therefore, when you go as an invited guest to banquets of priests, do not forget clerical honor, but show yourself modest and restrained in all things; and take care that neither your tongue nor your itching ears, that is, that neither you yourself detract from others, nor lend your hearing to those who detract. Know that everything you say about others is to be turned back upon yourself, and perhaps you will be found guilty in the very things that you were reproving in others. But perhaps you will say: I cannot do injury to those who report it, for anyone strives in vain who plans to stop the lips of all. What, then, is another's detraction to me? Surely I cannot forbid men to speak? But, as we said above, so present yourself before the detractor that he may learn to detract from no one, when he sees that you do not willingly hear what is being said. Solomon says: Do not associate with detractors, for their destruction will come suddenly. And who knows the ruin of both: of him, that is, who detracts, and of him who lends his ear to the detractor? Be mature in morals and manner of life, sparing and prudent in words, discreet in silence and taciturnity. Be diligent in investigating the mysteries of the Scriptures; and if anything doubtful occurs to you as you read, know that it must be referred to the interpretations of the elders. of the most ancient city of Trier, a school in which there is an abundance of learned men; to them, when questions are doubtful, you will be able to have recourse. Let gold not be dearer to you than knowledge, for the fruit of wisdom is eternal, but the use of riches is brief and momentary. Let there be no one who prevents salutary study: not mother, not brother, not sister. You, do the work of an evangelist; learn what you are to teach, lest you turn out to be a shepherd and an idol. You are one, and have no second: for whom, then, would you store up riches? Live temperately; do not frequent weddings and immoderate banquets, for they both strip the mind of virtues and render the purse empty of coins. Procure for yourself, from the alms offered, copies of divine Scripture, by whose constant reading, made learned, you may worthily instruct the people committed to you, and raise your own self by contemplation to heavenly things. Love the knowledge of the Scriptures, and it will exalt you before God and men. Do not consent to the pleasures of the flesh; restrain the impulse of fury; and never forget death.

What sort the priest ought to be in his inner conduct. Chapter 7.

Since, however, it is not enough for a minister of Christ to lead honorable conduct before men, unless he also strives to appear pure from every crime before God, I exhort you to direct your heart in the fear of the Almighty, and never admit any thoughts against God. For the priest of God must be holy in mind and body, and pure in thought. Hence the Lord says: Be holy, for I am holy, the Lord your God, who sanctify you. And Peter, the chief apostle, says: You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of acquisition, that you may proclaim the virtues of him who called you out of darkness into his wonderful light. Let charity hold the first place in your heart, for it is the fullness of the law and the completion of the prophets. For the greatest of all virtues is charity, which consists in love of God and neighbor.

God, however, is to be loved with the whole heart for his own sake, and one’s neighbor for God’s sake. No one truly loves God if he [unclear] hates his neighbor. For Christ is God and man. Therefore whoever hates man hates the whole Christ. God accepts no good work unless the flame of charity kindles it upon the altar of the heart. For charity holds the chief place among all the virtues. Humility follows it, which is remembered as the guardian of the virtues. So great is the eminence of this virtue that every other one quickly perishes unless it is strengthened on the foundation of humility. Saint Pope Gregory says: He who gathers virtues without humility carries dust into the wind. From the place where he is seen to carry something, there he is the more gravely blinded.

Therefore the greatest adornment of a priest is charity, and the most precious pearl in that splendid garment is humility. You too, brother, display these twin virtues in yourself, and you will be a fruitful preacher in the church of God. Whatever you say you will easily persuade your hearers, if you have charity and humility in your heart and diligently show them in your work. Let cursed ambition have no place in your heart; once it has invaded the mind, it so blinds it that it brings forgetfulness of God’s saving [unclear]. Be a Christian lover of men and an enemy of vices. Keep the commandments of God, and neglect none of the ecclesiastical sanctions. Honor all men for God’s sake, and judge no one at all to be despised. What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another. Let not the sun set upon your anger. Flee the flatteries of the rich, and never caress sinners. Deny your rash desires, so that you may become a disciple of Christ. Chastise your body, according to the apostle, bringing it back into servitude; despise delights; love chaste fasting. Be kind to the poor: feed the hungry, clothe the naked, visit the sick, free the captive, console the sorrowful, bury the dead. Love nothing in the world; seek no riches; run after no vanity. For no one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs. Do injury to no one, but learn to bear patiently what is inflicted, after the example of God, who, hanging on the cross, [prayed?] for his persecutors that they should not perish. Have peace with all men, but concord and unanimity only with the devout.

Do not be proud and arrogant, not sleepy and lazy, not given to wine and much eating, not a detractor and one who rashly judges anyone. Guard your actions at every hour, and let the memory of the things to come always turn in your thought. For Scripture says: Son, remember your last things, and you will not sin forever. Accordingly always think that you are going to die; fear the day of judgment; dread the torments of hell. If you do these things, you will easily overcome all temptations of the flesh. Despise the pleasures of the world, so that you may be able to enter rejoicing into the joys of heavenly happiness. Do not deceive your soul: no one can rejoice here with the world and afterward reign with Christ. For through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God. Therefore, with present things despised, let us hasten with all desire toward eternal joys. With all watchfulness guard your heart, since life proceeds from it. If you have been overtaken by some offense, do not delay in seeking the remedies of penitence, and in cleansing yourself in confession through true contrition. Strive to enter by the narrow way into life: that is, not to fulfill the desires of the flesh, to hate the world, to live in the spirit. You have been called to serve God as a soldier against the vices of the flesh; do not rest before victory, do not cease from the battle, for no one will be crowned unless he is victor. In this life, however, there is no certain victory, but continual battle. He who perseveres to the end will be saved. A man will be approved at his end. The life of man upon earth is warfare. For as a soldier of the highest king, it is not permitted you to abandon his contest. A good soldier follows his king wherever he goes. Where, then, is your king? In heaven. Why do you not follow him? What are you doing on earth, if you are a soldier of the heavenly king above? Why do you not follow your lord? He himself says: He who ministers to me, let him follow me; and where I am, there also my minister will be. Let him follow, he says, not with the steps of feet, but with the steps of affections. The apostle also says: No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has approved himself. Therefore, just as those who serve an earthly king obey all his commands, and wherever they are sent are ready and prompt,

excusing themselves on account of wife or children: so it is fitting for the soldier of Christ to obey his commands in all things, and in nothing at all to excuse himself. You therefore, who await the unfading crown of victory, toil like a good soldier of Jesus Christ: let no care of earthly anxiety weigh you down; let no enticement of fleshly pleasure touch your mind. For nothing is happier than the soldier of Christ, to whom the kingdoms of heaven are promised; nothing more toilsome, than one who daily runs risk of his life; nothing stronger, than one who conquers the devil; nothing weaker, than one who is overcome by the flesh. Let not home draw you away; let not kinship hinder you; let not the flesh constrain you. I wish you to be without anxiety, so that you may freely think on the things that are God’s. Naked and unencumbered fly to heaven, because naked your mother bore you, and naked the earth will receive you. Love what you cannot [unclear]; seek where you may rejoice happily for eternity. Live so that you do not fear to die. A good conscience does not fear death, because through it it knows that it will come to the eternal joys of the heavenly homeland. You now have, most beloved brother, what you asked of me; you have a certain pattern of good conduct on which you may imprint yourself; you have a rule of holy exhortation to which you may diligently have recourse. I have done what I could, not as much as I wished. For the rest, live according to the Gospel and the constitutions of the holy fathers, in which the whole form of Christian perfection is seen. Farewell, mindful of us. From Sponheim, on the Kalends of April, in the year 1486. Here ends the little book of lord Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, On the Life of Priests.
